titleEn: He raises the poor from the dust
progression: | G D | Em C | G D | G G |
intro: Nine verses, and the opening of Hallel, the run of Psalms 113 to 118 said on festivals, on Rosh Chodesh and at the seder, where this psalm and 114 come before the meal. It turns on one move: God is higher than everything there is, and what He does with that height is look downward. Two things for a learner. The imperative praise appears three times in verse 1 alone, and the psalm is closed at both ends by Hallelujah, so the first two words and the last two are the same. And five words here end in an extra yod that carries no meaning: the one who sits high, the one who bends low, the one who raises, the one who seats, the one who settles. It is an old poetic ending that Hebrew later dropped, so it looks like an error and is not.

stichs.en: Hallelujah.
Praise, servants of the LORD,
praise the name of the LORD.

verses.summary: Three imperatives in nine words, all the same form of the same verb. The ones told to praise are named as servants, which is the psalm's first hint that its subject is people at the bottom of an order.

stichs.en: Let the name of the LORD be blessed
from now and for ever.

verses.summary: The imperatives give way to a wish, and the psalm stretches out in time. Blessed is a passive participle, so the line never says who does the blessing, only that the name should stand blessed from this moment on.

stichs.en: From the rising of the sun to where it goes in,
the name of the LORD is praised.

verses.summary: Having stretched the praise across all time, the psalm stretches it across all space, and does it with the plainest available measure, the distance the sun travels in a day.

stichs.en: High above all nations is the LORD,
above the heavens His glory.

verses.summary: The height is stated twice and raised the second time, from over the nations to over the sky. Neither clause has a verb; the whole verse is position.

stichs.en: Who is like the LORD our God,
who sits so high,

verses.summary: A question that expects no answer, and then a participle that begins a sentence running through the next verse. The name here has a prefix meaning like, so the divine name is inside a comparison rather than standing alone.

stichs.en: who bends down low to look,
on the heavens and on the earth?

verses.summary: The turn of the whole psalm, in four words. The verb is the exact opposite of the one in verse 5, and the second half puts the heavens themselves among the things that have to be looked down at.

stichs.en: He raises the poor from the dust,
he lifts the needy from the ash heap,

verses.summary: The looking of verse 6 arrives somewhere. Two parallel clauses with the same shape, and the place named in the second is the rubbish tip outside a town, which is where the destitute actually lived.

stichs.en: to seat him with nobles,
with the nobles of His people.

verses.summary: The verb for sitting comes back from verse 5, where it belonged to God on the height. What was done to the man is that he was given the same posture.

stichs.en: who settles the barren woman in her house,
a glad mother of children.
Hallelujah.

verses.summary: The third reversal and the most concrete, and the verb for seating appears a third time. The psalm ends on the same two words it opened with, so the frame closes exactly.

pardes.body: Three movements of three verses. Verses 1 to 3 are about the name, praised by servants, blessed through all time, praised across the whole width of the day. Verses 4 to 6 are about height, and they turn in the middle: {{5.3}} and {{6.0}} are two participles in the same unusual form, one going up and one going down, and that pair is the psalm's whole argument. Verses 7 to 9 are what the downward look reaches, three people at the bottom, the poor, the needy and the barren woman, each of them moved. Note that the verb for sitting runs through all three movements, from the one seated on high in verse 5 to the man seated with nobles in verse 8 to the woman settled in a house in verse 9.

Five words in this psalm carry a yod on the end that adds no meaning and changes no grammar: {{5.3}}, {{6.0}}, {{7.0}}, {{8.0}} and {{9.0}}. It is an old ending, found mostly in poetry, and its density here is unusual even for the Psalms. The second thing to notice is that verses 7 and 8 are close to a line in Hannah's song at 1 Samuel 2:8, which also raises the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap and seats them with nobles, and verse 9 is close to 1 Samuel 2:5 on the barren woman. Whether the psalm quotes the song, the song quotes the psalm, or both draw on a formula older than either is disputed and the evidence does not settle it. One last thing: {{9.1}} literally means the barren one of the house, and modern Hebrew took the same two words and made them mean the woman who runs the household, which reverses the sense the psalm gives them.

The last line of this psalm is the subject of a recorded dispute. Mishnah Pesachim 10:6 asks how far Hallel is recited before the meal at the seder: the school of Shammai says as far as {{9.3}} to {{9.5}}, a glad mother of children, which is the end of Psalm 113, and the school of Hillel says as far as the end of Psalm 114. The practice follows Hillel, so the psalm is not read alone there. The reason the question is live is that the barren woman made a mother is the standard image of a reversal that nobody could have arranged, which makes it either a fitting place to stop before the meal or an incomplete thought that needs the exodus of Psalm 114 to finish it.

The two participles at {{5.3}} and {{6.0}} are the verse the mystical reading works on. A God defined by being high who is then defined by bending down is a contradiction only if height means distance, and the kabbalistic answer is contraction: the infinite makes room by withdrawing, and what looks like descent is the condition for anything small existing at all. On that reading verses 7 to 9 are not three examples of charity but three demonstrations of the same mechanism, since dust, ash heap and barrenness are all names for a place with nothing in it. The barren woman at {{9.1}} is read in this tradition as the exiled community, on the strength of Isaiah 54:1, where Zion is addressed as the barren one and told to sing.
